→ The law said: even though the company itself didn't commit the act, it is held responsible because the employee worked for them.

"The lawyer's knowledge is imputed to the client."
→ Whatever the lawyer knew is legally treated as though the client also knew it, because the lawyer represents them.

This is called imputed liability or imputed knowledge — the idea that legal responsibility can be transferred or assigned to you through your connection to another party.

3. Theological Use

In Christian theology, "impute" carries a very specific and important meaning. It refers to God officially crediting something to a person's account — not because they earned it, but by divine declaration.

"Adam's sin was imputed to all of humanity."
→ All humans are considered to share in the guilt of Adam's original sin, even though they weren't there.

"The righteousness of Christ is imputed to the believer."
→ God treats the believer as righteous — not because they earned it, but because Christ's perfect righteousness is credited to them.

Here, "impute" is almost an accounting term used in a spiritual sense: something is put on your account.

4. Economic / Statistical Use

In economics and statistics, "impute" means to estimate and assign a value to something that doesn't have a directly measurable or visible price.

"Economists impute a value to unpaid household labor."
→ Since no one pays you to cook or clean your own home, economists calculate and assign an estimated dollar value to that work anyway.

A common example is imputed rent: if you own the home you live in, economists assign a theoretical "rent" value — what you would pay if you were renting — to account for the economic value of that housing.

Here, "impute" simply means: we don't have a direct number, so we assign a reasonable estimate.

• It does not mean to physically give something to someone.
  • It does not mean to punish someone directly.
  • It does not always mean the accusation is true — you can wrongly impute a fault to someone.
  • It is not the same as "compute" or "input" (two words that look and sound similar but are completely unrelated).

Imputation (noun) — the act or result of imputing something.
"He rejected the imputation of cowardice." → He rejected the claim that he was a coward.

Imputed (adjective) — used especially in legal and economic phrases.
"Imputed income," "imputed liability," "imputed knowledge" — all mean values or responsibilities that are assigned rather than directly earned or proven.

To impute is to officially place something on someone — a fault, a motive, a responsibility, or a value — based on reasoning, relationship, or formal rules, even when it isn't directly visible or proven. In everyday life, it means to read blame or bad intent into someone's actions. In law, it means holding someone responsible for what others in their circle did. In theology, it means God crediting something to a person's moral account. In economics, it means assigning a calculated value to something without a market price.

The common thread across all these uses: you are assigning something intangible to someone — placing it on them by judgment or rule, not by handing it over physically.
8259:
When someone is "in a flap," they are in a state of anxiety, panic, or agitation about something. They feel nervous, flustered, and unsettled — often to the point where they don't quite know what to do with themselves.

Think of it this way: imagine someone rushing around the house, worrying loudly, unable to sit still, overthinking everything — that person is "in a flap."

"She was in a complete flap before her job interview."

This means she was very anxious and worked up about it.
The Feeling It Describes — More Precisely

Being "in a flap" is not just simple worry. It captures a particular kind of flustered, restless panic — the kind where your mind is racing, you may be overreacting a little, and you can't seem to calm yourself down. It often suggests that the person's panic is slightly disproportionate to the actual problem, though not always.

It is different from being quietly worried. It has an element of visible, outward agitation — the person seems unsettled to others around them, not just on the inside.
Where Does It Come From?

The idiom comes from the image of a bird flapping its wings in a panic.

When a bird is suddenly startled or frightened, it flaps its wings rapidly and frantically in all directions — it looks chaotic, uncontrolled, and alarmed. This visual of frantic, uncoordinated movement was adopted into everyday English to describe a person who is similarly flustered and anxious.

The word "flap" on its own has carried the meaning of a state of panic or excitement in English since at least the late 19th century, and the phrase "in a flap" grew naturally from this.

So the next time you picture someone "in a flap," imagine a startled bird wildly beating its wings — and then picture a person behaving emotionally the same way.
Is It British or American?

This is primarily a British English idiom. You will hear it very commonly in the UK, Ireland, and Australia. While Americans can understand it, they are far less likely to use it in natural conversation. Americans are more likely to say things like "in a panic," "freaking out," or "all worked up."

So if you are learning British English, this is a very useful and natural phrase to know. If you are learning American English, it is still worth knowing so you can understand it when you come across it.
Register — Formal or Informal?

"In a flap" is informal and conversational. You would use it in:

  • Everyday conversations with friends or family
  • Casual writing, texting, or social media
  • Informal workplace chat

You would not use it in:

  • Formal essays or academic writing
  • Professional reports or official communications
  • Job applications or formal emails
How to Use It in a Sentence

The phrase is very flexible. Here are the main patterns:

Pattern 1: "be in a flap" (describing a current state)

"He is in a complete flap about the dinner party tonight."
"Why are you in such a flap?"

Pattern 2: "get in a flap" (describing the process of becoming anxious)

"She always gets in a flap before exams."
"Don't get in a flap — there's still plenty of time."

Pattern 3: "cause a flap" / "create a flap" (describing something that caused panic or fuss)

"The sudden change in plans caused quite a flap at the office."

Notice that you can intensify it with words like "complete," "total," or "such a" to show the panic is strong:

"He was in a total flap."
"Stop being in such a flap!"
Real-Life Examples to Make It Stick

Here are some vivid, relatable situations to cement the meaning:

  • Your friend has guests coming in one hour and the house is messy, the food isn't ready, and she's rushing around bumping into things — she's in a flap.
  • Your colleague can't find an important document right before a big meeting and is pacing around nervously — he's in a flap.
  • A student suddenly realizes an assignment is due tomorrow and starts panicking, unable to decide where to begin — they're in a flap.
  • A dad is trying to pack the car for a family trip, everyone is talking at once, and he can't remember if he turned off the stove — he's in a total flap.
The Subtle Nuance — Don't Miss This

A small but important detail: when you say someone is "in a flap," there is often a gentle, slightly humorous undertone to it. It can subtly suggest that the person is overreacting a bit and that things are probably not as bad as they think. It's not a harsh or mean thing to say — it's usually affectionate or mildly teasing.

For example, if a friend says:

"Oh, don't be in such a flap — it's just a small scratch on the car!"

They're kindly saying: calm down, you're panicking more than you need to.

However, this nuance is not always present. Sometimes people use it to describe genuine, justified anxiety, with no suggestion of overreaction. Context will tell you which is which.
Similar Idioms and Phrases

Knowing related expressions will help you understand the full landscape of this meaning in English:

  • "In a tizzy" — very similar; flustered and worked up (also more British)
  • "In a state" — anxious and upset (e.g., "She was in a right state.")
  • "In a panic" — more universal; straightforward panic
  • "All worked up" — emotionally agitated and anxious
  • "In a stew" — worried and troubled about something (older expression)
  • "Hot and bothered" — flustered, anxious, or upset
  • "Up in arms" — angry and outraged (slightly different — more about anger than anxiety)
  • "On edge" — nervously tense and easily startled

Among all of these, "in a flap" stands out for its image of visible, restless, bird-like agitation — it's more vivid and more specifically British than most of the others.
What It Does NOT Mean

To make sure there's no confusion:

  • It does not mean physically flapping something with your hands (though that image inspired it).
  • It does not mean angry — it's about anxiety and panic, not rage.
  • It does not mean sad or depressed — it's an active, restless, agitated state, not a low-energy one.
  • It does not necessarily mean the problem is small — though it can imply that.
Quick Summary

MeaningIn a state of anxiety, panic, or flustered agitation
OriginA bird flapping its wings in fright
RegisterInformal / conversational
Common inBritish, Irish, and Australian English
ToneOften slightly affectionate or humorous
Key patternsbe in a flap, get in a flap, cause a flap

You now have everything you need to fully understand, recognize, and correctly use the idiom "in a flap" — in any context you encounter it.
8260:
To be "in a funk" means to feel sad, gloomy, unmotivated, or emotionally low — not because of one sharp, clear reason, but more like a heavy cloud of dullness has settled over you. It is a general feeling of being stuck in a low mood.

Think of it this way: it is not the sharp pain of a broken bone. It is more like carrying a heavy backpack all day — you are not injured, but everything feels harder, slower, and less enjoyable than usual.

"I've been in a funk all week. I don't even feel like watching TV."
The Two Main Shades of Meaning

This idiom carries two closely related but slightly different uses, and understanding both will make you fluent in its usage.

1. An emotional funk — feeling sad or gloomy

This is the most common use. The person feels low, flat, or melancholy. They are not in a crisis, but they are not okay either. They may feel disconnected from joy, quiet, withdrawn, or just "off."

"Ever since her best friend moved away, she's been in a funk."
"He seemed fine at breakfast, but by evening he was clearly in a funk."

2. A creative or motivational funk — feeling stuck or uninspired

Here, "funk" refers to a block or slump in productivity, creativity, or drive. An artist, writer, athlete, or student might use this when they cannot seem to get going, even when they want to.

"The novelist was in a funk for three months and couldn't write a single page."
"After the injury, the basketball player was in a scoring funk for several games."

Both meanings share the same core idea: a state of being stuck in something low, whether it is your mood or your performance.

Understanding what this idiom does not mean is just as important.

  • It is not clinical depression. A funk is temporary and mild by comparison. Depression is a serious medical condition. People sometimes use the word casually, but the idiom itself describes something passing and less severe.
  • It is not a sudden, sharp emotion like anger or grief. A funk is more like a slow, lingering fog.
  • It is not used for physical illness. If someone has a fever, you would not say they are "in a funk."
Where Does the Word "Funk" Come From?

The word "funk" has an interesting history that helps the meaning click.

It is believed to come from the Flemish word fonck, meaning fear, distress, or panic. In early English usage (around the 1700s), a "funk" described a state of fear or nervous agitation — you were in a funk if you were terrified of something.

Over time, the meaning softened and shifted. Instead of fear, it came to describe a general state of emotional gloom, depression, or low spirits. By the 1800s, it was widely used in English to describe exactly what we use it for today — that heavy, listless, gloomy feeling.

So the idiom evolved from "paralysed by fear" → "weighed down by low spirits" → the modern meaning of a general emotional or motivational slump.

(Note: "Funk" also exists as a music genre — think James Brown. That word has a completely separate African-American cultural origin and is unrelated to this idiom.)
The Tone and Feel of This Idiom

"In a funk" is:

  • Informal and conversational. You would say this to a friend, a family member, or a colleague you are close with. You would not use it in a formal business report or an academic essay.
  • Sympathetic in tone. When someone says another person is "in a funk," it is usually said with understanding and concern, not judgment.
  • Vague by nature. Part of what makes this idiom so useful is that it does not demand a specific reason. You can be in a funk for no particular reason, and the phrase perfectly captures that foggy, unexplained low.
How to Use It Naturally — More Examples

Here are examples across different situations so you can see the idiom in action:

Talking about yourself:

"I've been in a bit of a funk lately. I think I just need a proper holiday."
"I don't know what's wrong with me — I've been in a funk since Monday."

Talking about someone else:

"She's in a funk because her job interview didn't go well."
"Don't take it personally if he's quiet — he's been in a funk this week."

Talking about creative or professional performance:

"The whole team is in a funk after losing three matches in a row."
"She was in a creative funk, but a trip to the countryside helped her get back on track."

Getting out of a funk:

"A good night's sleep and a long walk finally snapped me out of my funk."
"He got out of his funk after talking to an old friend."

Notice the natural phrases: you are in a funk, you get out of a funk, or someone snaps you out of your funk.

These idioms carry a very similar meaning and are often used interchangeably:

  • "Down in the dumps" — feeling sad and low
  • "Feeling blue" — feeling sad or melancholy
  • "In a slump" — performing poorly or feeling uninspired (especially in sports/work)
  • "Out of sorts" — feeling slightly unwell or irritable and low
  • "Under a cloud" — feeling gloomy, often with a sense of worry hanging over you

"In a funk" sits comfortably among all of these, but it carries a slightly stronger suggestion of listlessness and being emotionally stuck than some of the others.
A Quick Summary to Lock It In

Core meaningFeeling sad, low, gloomy, or unmotivated — like a temporary emotional or creative slump
SeverityMild to moderate — not a crisis, but not fine either
DurationTemporary — a funk passes
RegisterInformal and casual
Key phrasesin a funk, get out of a funk, snap out of a funk

The beauty of this idiom is how perfectly it captures a feeling that is hard to explain — that frustrating, foggy, "I don't know what's wrong but nothing feels right" state that every human being experiences from time to time. Now you have the language to name it precisely.
8261:
When something is "in abeyance," it means it is temporarily paused, suspended, or put on hold — but not cancelled or ended permanently. The key idea is that it is expected to resume or become active again at some point in the future.

Think of it as pressing the pause button on something. The thing still exists, it hasn't gone away, but it is simply not moving forward right now.

Imagine you and a friend are playing a board game. Halfway through, you both need to leave for dinner. You don't throw the game away — you leave the pieces exactly where they are and plan to come back later.

That game, while you're at dinner, is in abeyance. It is waiting. It's paused. It will pick up again.

The word "abeyance" came into English from the Old French word abeance, which meant a state of longing, expectation, or waiting — almost like holding your breath for something. It entered English in the 16th century and was first used heavily in legal language (more on that below). Over time, it spread into general formal writing.

The idea of waiting with expectation is baked right into the word's DNA, which is why "in abeyance" always carries that sense that something will eventually return.
The Full Nuance — What Makes It Precise

This is where most learners stop reading, but this section is what separates a vague understanding from a sharp one.

"In abeyance" has three layers you must understand to use it correctly:

1. It is temporary, not permanent.
If something is cancelled forever, you would never say it is "in abeyance." That word is exclusively for situations where there is a real possibility — or strong expectation — that it will resume.

2. It involves inactivity, not slow progress.
Something "in abeyance" is not moving slowly. It has completely stopped for the time being. There is a full pause.

3. It is usually outside the control of one person.
Things are typically put "in abeyance" because of external circumstances — waiting for a decision, waiting for funds, waiting for a law to be settled, waiting for a situation to resolve. It carries a slightly formal, serious tone.
Its Natural Home: Formal and Legal Language

"In abeyance" is not casual conversation language. You would almost never hear someone say it in small talk. It lives comfortably in:

  • Legal documents and court judgments
  • Government and policy writing
  • Business and corporate language
  • Formal journalism and news reporting
  • Academic writing

In law specifically, "in abeyance" has a very precise technical meaning: it refers to a situation where ownership of property or a legal title has no current owner and is simply waiting for the rightful person to come forward or be determined. For example, if a noble title has no living heir to claim it, the title is said to be "in abeyance" — suspended, unclaimed, but not extinct.

These examples go from simple to more complex so you can see the full range of the idiom:

"The road construction project is in abeyance until the city approves the new budget."

(The project has stopped temporarily and will restart once money is confirmed.)

"Their plans to move abroad were held in abeyance while her mother recovered from surgery."

(They put their plans on pause for a personal reason, planning to revisit them later.)

"The new policy was placed in abeyance pending a full review by the committee."

(The policy exists but has been frozen — it is not being enforced until the review is done.)

"During the peace talks, military operations were held in abeyance."

(Fighting was paused, not ended, while negotiations continued.)

"The disputed title to the land remains in abeyance until the court delivers its verdict."

(No one can claim the land right now because it is legally unresolved and waiting.)

Notice that "in abeyance" almost always follows a small set of verbs:

  • held in abeyance — the most common pairing
  • placed in abeyance
  • kept in abeyance
  • remain(s) in abeyance
  • fall into abeyance — this one is slightly different (see below)

"Fall into abeyance" deserves special mention. It means something that was once active has gradually become inactive or has been forgotten over time — like an old law that nobody enforces anymore, or a tradition that people slowly stopped following. It doesn't necessarily mean it will come back.

"The old custom of bowing when entering the hall had fallen into abeyance by the 20th century."
How It Differs From Similar Words

ConceptKey Difference
On holdSame idea, but far more casual and informal. Use "on hold" in everyday speech; use "in abeyance" in formal writing.
SuspendedImplies a deliberate decision by someone in authority and can feel more permanent or punitive. A person's license can be "suspended." A project is usually "in abeyance."
DormantSuggests something is sleeping and may or may not wake up. "Dormant" leans more toward inactivity with no guarantee of return. "In abeyance" leans toward expected return.
Pending"Pending" means waiting for something specific to happen (like an approval). "In abeyance" means paused — the trigger for its return may not even be defined yet.

If you want a simple mental hook:

"In abeyance = In the waiting room."

Something in a waiting room hasn't gone home. It hasn't been turned away. It is simply waiting for its turn to be called back in. That is exactly the feeling of "in abeyance."

• Meaning: Temporarily paused or suspended, with the expectation of resuming later.
  • Tone: Formal. Used in legal, governmental, business, and journalistic contexts.
  • Key distinction: Always temporary. Always carries a sense that it may return.
  • Most common phrase: "held in abeyance"
  • Special use: In law, it refers to a title or property with no current owner, waiting to be claimed.
  • "Fall into abeyance" means something has gradually become inactive or forgotten over time.
8262:
In absentia means while not being physically present — specifically at a formal event, official proceeding, or ceremony that directly concerns the person who is absent.

When something is done "in absentia," it means:

A formal action was carried out about someone, or on behalf of someone, even though that person was not there to witness or participate in it.

The action still counts. It is still official. It still has real consequences for the person. Their absence did not stop it from happening, and it did not make the outcome any less valid.

The phrase does two things at once — it acknowledges that someone is absent, and it confirms that the proceedings went ahead anyway, fully and officially, without them.

Think of it this way: normally, you'd expect the person to be there. Their presence would be the natural, expected thing. But for some reason — they fled, they refused to come, they were ill, they were far away, or they simply chose not to attend — they weren't there. And yet, the event happened, the decision was made, and the result applies to them just as much as if they had been sitting right there in the room.
Where You Will See It Used

In absentia appears almost exclusively in formal, official contexts. Here are the two most common ones:

1. Legal proceedings

This is where the phrase is used most powerfully. A person accused of a crime has the right to be present at their own trial. But sometimes they run away, or deliberately refuse to appear in court. In many legal systems, the court can proceed anyway. If the person is found guilty, they are said to have been convicted in absentia — meaning the verdict was reached and handed down without them ever stepping foot in the courtroom.

Example: "The drug lord fled the country before his trial began. He was convicted in absentia and sentenced to 30 years in prison."

The sentence is real. The conviction is real. The fact that he wasn't there doesn't erase it.

2. Academic ceremonies

Universities hold graduation ceremonies where students walk across a stage to receive their degrees. But sometimes a graduate cannot attend — they live on the other side of the world, they are seriously ill, they are serving in the military, or there is a family emergency. Many universities will still formally award the degree during the ceremony even without the student present. The student is said to have received their degree in absentia.

Example: "She had already moved abroad for work, so her degree was awarded in absentia at the May ceremony."

The degree is just as real and valid as everyone else's.

Not every absence qualifies for this phrase. You would not say you watched a movie in absentia or that someone missed a birthday party in absentia. The phrase is reserved for formal, official proceedings where the person is the direct subject — where the event is about them, for them, or against them in some official capacity.

The absent person has a stake in what is happening. Something is being decided, granted, or ruled upon that directly affects their life, their status, or their rights. That is what makes their absence noteworthy enough to name.
How It Works as an Adverb

As an adverb, in absentia modifies a verb — it tells you how or under what condition the action was performed.

  • "He was tried in absentia." (The trying happened — but without him present.)
  • "She was sentenced in absentia." (The sentencing happened — but without her present.)
  • "The honor was bestowed in absentia." (The honor was given — but without the recipient there.)

In every case, the adverb is quietly telling you: yes, this really happened, and yes, it counts — even without the person being there.

If you ever need to recall what this phrase means, come back to this:

"In absentia" means that a formal, official action was carried out about a person — completely and validly — despite the fact that they were not physically present."

That's the whole idea. Everything else is just context.
8263:
"In all likelihood" means "very probably" or "most likely."

When you say something is true in all likelihood, you are saying that based on what you know, the evidence, or common sense — something is very likely to happen or to be true — though you are not 100% certain.

Think of it this way:

You are not guaranteeing something. You are making a very strong, confident prediction based on the information available to you.

Understanding the individual words helps the meaning stick forever.

"Likelihood" means probability or chance. It comes from the word "likely" (meaning probable) + the suffix "-hood" (which means "a state or condition" — just like childhood means the state of being a child, likelihood means the state of being likely/probable).

"In all likelihood" literally means "considering all the probability" or "taking all the chances into account." In other words: when you weigh everything up, something is very probably true.
The Core Idea (The Heart of the Idiom)

This idiom sits in a specific zone of certainty. Imagine a scale:

  • Impossible → Unlikely → Possible → Likely → Very likely → Certain

"In all likelihood" lives close to the "certain" end — but it never quite reaches it. It says: "I'm not 100% sure, but I'm very, very confident."

This is what makes it different from saying "definitely" or "certainly." You leave just a tiny crack of doubt open, which is actually the honest and accurate thing to do in most real-life situations.

Here are sentences that show how the idiom is naturally used:

  1. "In all likelihood, it will rain this evening."

(The clouds look dark, the forecast says so — rain is very probable.)

  1. "She studied hard every day, so in all likelihood, she will pass the exam."

(Based on her effort and preparation, passing is the most probable outcome.)

  1. "The flight is delayed by three hours. In all likelihood, we will miss our connection."

(Given the delay, missing the connection is almost certain.)

  1. "He hasn't replied in two days. In all likelihood, he didn't receive your message."

(The most logical and probable explanation is that the message wasn't received.)

  1. "This medicine will, in all likelihood, reduce your symptoms within a week."

(Doctors use this kind of phrasing to be honest — it's very probable, but not guaranteed.)
Where in a Sentence Can You Place It?

This is an adverbial phrase, which means it describes or modifies the probability of the whole statement. The good news is it's quite flexible in placement.

At the beginning (most common):

"In all likelihood, the match will be postponed."

In the middle of the sentence:

"The match will, in all likelihood, be postponed."

(Notice the commas on both sides when it's placed in the middle — this is important.)

At the end (less common, but correct):

"The match will be postponed, in all likelihood."

All three mean exactly the same thing. Placing it at the beginning gives it a slightly more formal or emphatic feel, while putting it in the middle feels more conversational and smooth.
What Kind of Language Is It? (Register/Tone)

"In all likelihood" is slightly formal. You'll commonly find it in:

  • News articles and journalism
  • Academic and professional writing
  • Formal speeches
  • Thoughtful, educated conversation

In casual everyday speech, people often replace it with simpler words like "probably" or "most likely." But "in all likelihood" carries a more sophisticated and considered tone — it suggests that the speaker has thought something through before stating their conclusion.

These phrases carry a very similar meaning and can often be used in place of "in all likelihood":

  • "In all probability" — Nearly identical in meaning and tone. ("In all probability, he has already left.")
  • "Most likely" — Slightly less formal but means the same. ("She'll most likely be late.")
  • "Very probably" — Direct and simple. ("He very probably forgot.")
  • "Chances are" — More casual and conversational. ("Chances are, they already know.")
  • "It's highly likely that" — Formal and explicit. ("It's highly likely that prices will rise.")
How Is It Different from Similar Words?

PhraseDegree of Certainty

"Possibly" suggests only a weak chance — maybe yes, maybe no. It's much weaker than "in all likelihood."

"Probably" is the everyday, casual version of "in all likelihood." They mean nearly the same thing, but "in all likelihood" sounds more thoughtful and formal.

"Certainly" / "Definitely" leave zero room for doubt. "In all likelihood" always leaves a small but honest margin of uncertainty — which is actually what makes it more precise and trustworthy in many situations.

"Inevitably" means it will happen — there is no other possibility. "In all likelihood" never claims that level of certainty.

Do not confuse "in all likelihood" with meaning something is guaranteed. It always signals a strong probability, not a certainty. The moment you are 100% certain about something, you should use words like "certainly," "without doubt," or "definitely" instead.

Also, when you place it in the middle of a sentence, always put commas on both sides of it:

✅ "The results will, in all likelihood, be announced tomorrow."
❌ "The results will in all likelihood be announced tomorrow." (Missing commas make it harder to read.)

"In all likelihood" = "Based on everything we know, this is very probably true or going to happen — though I can't be 100% certain."

It is a confident, honest, and slightly formal way of expressing a strong probability, without overreaching into false certainty.
8264:
"In anticipation of" means: because you expect something to happen.

It describes an action, decision, or feeling that occurs before an expected event, and is caused by the expectation of that event.

There are always two layers working together:

  • Time: the action happens before the expected event
  • Reason: the action happens because of the expectation

Both layers are always present. That's what makes this phrase precise.

"She bought extra water in anticipation of the storm."

Break it down:

  • She expected the storm to come.
  • Before it arrived, and because she expected it, she bought extra water.

You could rewrite this as: "She bought extra water because she expected the storm."

That's essentially what "in anticipation of" means — but it's more formal and more compact.
It Works for Actions and for Feelings

For actions (doing something):

"The company hired more staff in anticipation of rapid growth."

→ They expected growth. Before it happened, they hired people because of that expectation.

"They evacuated the city in anticipation of the hurricane."

→ The hurricane hadn't arrived yet. They left because they expected it.

For emotions and mental states (feeling something):

"He was quiet and nervous in anticipation of the surgery."

→ He wasn't doing anything specific — he was feeling something, caused by expecting the surgery.

"The children could hardly sleep in anticipation of Christmas morning."

→ Their excitement came from expecting Christmas. The expectation itself caused the sleeplessness.

This is an important point: "in anticipation of" isn't limited to practical actions. It also captures the inner emotional state that arises from expecting something.
It Works for Good and Bad Expected Events

Expected event is good:

"She prepared a speech in anticipation of winning the award."

Expected event is bad or difficult:

"The hospital called in extra staff in anticipation of a surge in patients."

Expected event is neutral:

"The hotel prepared extra rooms in anticipation of the conference."

The phrase itself doesn't judge whether the expected event is good or bad — it simply points to the expectation as the cause of the current action or feeling.

"In anticipation of" must be followed by a noun or a noun phrase (a word or group of words that acts as a noun).

✅ "in anticipation of the announcement"
✅ "in anticipation of her return"
✅ "in anticipation of a large crowd"
✅ "in anticipation of receiving the results" (gerund phrase — "receiving" acts as a noun here)
How It Differs From Similar Phrases

Understanding the differences sharpens your grasp of the phrase.

"In anticipation of" vs. "because of"

"Because of" refers to something that already happened.
"In anticipation of" refers to something expected to happen (it hasn't occurred yet).

"She was relieved because of the good news." → The news already came.
"She was tense in anticipation of the news." → The news hasn't come yet.

"In anticipation of" vs. "before"

"Before" only tells you when something happened — it doesn't explain why.
"In anticipation of" tells you both — when (before the event) and why (because of the expectation).

"He packed his bags before the trip." → Just a time relationship. He could have packed for any reason.
"He packed his bags in anticipation of leaving." → He packed because he expected to leave. The expectation is the reason.

"In anticipation of" vs. "in preparation for"

These two are the closest to each other, and they often overlap. But there's a subtle difference:

"In preparation for" focuses on the practical act of getting ready. It's about the doing.
"In anticipation of" focuses more on the expectation driving the action or feeling. It can describe both practical preparation and pure emotional states.

"She trained hard in preparation for the marathon." → Focus: the practical training activity.
"She was anxious in anticipation of the marathon." → Focus: the expectation causing a feeling.

You can sometimes use them interchangeably for preparatory actions, but "in anticipation of" is the only one that also works for pure emotional or mental states.

"In anticipation of" is a formal phrase. You'll find it in:

  • Business emails and reports
  • Official announcements
  • News writing and journalism
  • Formal speeches
  • Academic and professional writing

In everyday casual conversation, people would more naturally say:

  • "because she knew it was coming..."
  • "expecting the storm, she..."
  • "getting ready for..."

But whenever you're writing or speaking in a formal context, "in anticipation of" is exactly the right level of language.

"In anticipation of" = before something expected, and because of that expectation.

It describes an action, decision, or feeling that:

  1. Happens before a future event
  2. Is caused or motivated by expecting that future event

It works equally for practical preparations ("they stocked supplies in anticipation of the flood") and for emotional states ("she was trembling in anticipation of the performance"). It always points to the expectation as the driving force behind whatever is happening now.
8265:
"In arrears" essentially means behind on something — most often, behind on a payment. The word "arrears" itself comes from the Old French word arrière, meaning "behind" or "at the back." Think of it like being at the back of a line when you were supposed to be at the front.

But here's what makes this term interesting: it has two related but distinct uses, and confusing them is one of the most common mistakes people make. Understanding both is the key to truly grasping the term.
Use #1 — The Everyday Meaning: You're Late and You Owe Money

In everyday language, being "in arrears" means you had an obligation to pay something by a certain date, and you didn't. The unpaid amount builds up, and that accumulated debt is called your arrears.

For example: If your rent is due on the 1st of every month, and you haven't paid for three months, you are three months in arrears. The total unpaid rent — say, $3,000 — is your arrears.

This is the meaning most people encounter first, and it carries a negative weight. Being in arrears means you've fallen behind, which can have real consequences like penalties, legal action, or damage to your credit score.

Common situations where this meaning applies:

Rent arrears: A tenant who hasn't paid rent on time is in rent arrears. Landlords can begin eviction proceedings once arrears reach a certain threshold.

Mortgage arrears: If you miss one or more mortgage payments, your lender considers you in arrears. This can eventually lead to foreclosure if not resolved.

Child support arrears: When a court orders a parent to pay child support and they don't, the unpaid amount accumulates as arrears. Courts treat this very seriously.

Tax arrears: Unpaid taxes owed to the government — whether income tax, property tax, or any other — are tax arrears.

Loan arrears: Missing monthly loan repayments puts you in arrears with your lender, which typically triggers late fees and can hurt your credit rating.

The key point here: arrears are overdue. Something was supposed to be paid, and it wasn't.
Use #2 — The Technical/Financial Meaning: Paying After the Fact (By Design)

This is where things get more nuanced, and where many learners get tripped up.

In finance and accounting, "in arrears" is also used to describe a payment structure where payment is intentionally made after a service or period has been completed — not because someone is late, but because that's how the arrangement was designed from the start.

This is the opposite of paying in advance (where you pay before receiving something).

The clearest example is your salary.

Most people in the world are paid in arrears. You work all of January, and then at the end of January — or even in early February — you receive your paycheck for January's work. You delivered the service (your labor) first, and the payment came afterward. Nobody is being irresponsible or delinquent here. It's simply a system where payment follows the completed work period.

This matters enormously because when a company says "we pay in arrears," they are not saying they pay late in a bad way — they are describing a deliberate, structured payment schedule where the payment period closes first, and then the payment is processed.

More examples of "in arrears" as a payment structure:

Utility bills: You use electricity, water, or gas throughout the month, and at the end of the month you receive a bill for what you consumed. You're paying in arrears — after the service was used.

Mortgage interest: Most mortgage interest is calculated and charged in arrears. You borrow money and use it throughout the month, then at the end of the month you pay the interest that accrued.

Annuities: An ordinary annuity (also called an annuity in arrears) makes payments at the end of each period. A bond that pays interest at the end of each year is an annuity in arrears. By contrast, an annuity due pays at the beginning of each period.

Preferred stock dividends: When a company fails to pay dividends on preferred shares, those unpaid dividends accumulate "in arrears." Crucially, most preferred shares are cumulative, meaning the company must pay all accumulated dividend arrears before it can pay any dividends to ordinary/common shareholders.
"In Arrears" vs. "In Advance" — The Clearest Way to Understand the Difference

Imagine you hire a plumber for a month-long project.

  • Paid in advance: You pay the plumber at the start of the month, before any work is done.
  • Paid in arrears: You pay the plumber at the end of the month, after all the work is complete.

Neither is wrong — they're simply different agreements. Most professional services and employment are structured as "in arrears" arrangements. Most subscriptions and rent agreements, interestingly, are often structured as "in advance" — you pay your rent for April at the beginning of April, before you've lived there for the month.

This is also why the phrase matters in contracts. A contract that specifies "payments due in arrears" means the payment clock starts after the service is rendered. A contract that says "payments due in advance" means the money is expected upfront.
How to Tell Which Meaning Is Being Used

Here's a simple rule of thumb:

  • If someone says a person or entity is in arrears (e.g., "He is in arrears on his mortgage"), it almost always means the negative sense — they're behind, they owe money they haven't paid.
  • If something is described as being paid in arrears (e.g., "Employees are paid in arrears"), it usually means the neutral, structural sense — payment comes after the period or service is completed, and that's the intended design.

Context is everything with this term.
What Happens When You Fall Into Arrears (The Negative Kind)

Falling into arrears on a debt or obligation can trigger a cascade of consequences, so it's worth understanding the typical sequence:

1. Missed payment: You miss a due date. The unpaid amount is now in arrears.

2. Late fees and penalties: Most lenders and landlords charge a penalty for late payment, often a flat fee or a percentage of the amount owed.

3. Interest on arrears: Some contracts charge extra interest on the overdue amount, making the arrears grow over time.

4. Formal notices: After a certain number of missed payments, you may receive a formal demand letter or notice of default.

5. Credit impact: Missed payments are typically reported to credit bureaus, damaging your credit score and making it harder to borrow in the future.

6. Legal action: In serious cases — particularly with mortgages, taxes, or child support — creditors or courts can take legal steps like foreclosure, liens on property, wage garnishment, or even imprisonment (in the case of child support in some jurisdictions).

The earlier you address arrears, the easier they are to resolve. Many lenders have hardship programs or restructuring options for borrowers who reach out proactively.
A Mental Model to Remember This Forever

Picture a race. The payment has a finishing line it needs to cross by a certain time.

  • On time: Payment crosses the finish line exactly when expected. ✅
  • In arrears (negative sense): The payment is lagging behind, still running the race when it should have already finished. ❌ — overdue.
  • In arrears (structural sense): The race was always designed so that the finish line comes after the work lap. ✅ — intentional, normal, expected.

The word "arrears" always means "behind." The only question is whether being behind is a failure (missed obligation) or a feature (the agreed-upon structure).

"In arrears" means behind in time — specifically, a payment that either hasn't been made when it should have (a problem), or is deliberately structured to come after a service or period is completed (by design). The word "arrears" refers to the accumulated unpaid or outstanding amount. Whether the term signals a financial emergency or a routine payroll process depends entirely on the context in which it's used — and now you have all the tools to tell the difference.
8266:
When two or more people are "in cahoots," they are secretly working together — usually to do something dishonest, unfair, or sneaky.

Think of it this way: imagine two people whispering in a corner, cooking up a secret plan that benefits themselves but harms or tricks others. That is the image "in cahoots" paints.

The most important things baked into this phrase are:

  • Secrecy — the partnership is hidden from others.
  • Joint involvement — at least two people are involved.
  • A negative purpose — it almost always involves something shady, corrupt, or deceptive.

The phrase always follows this pattern:

[Person A] is in cahoots with [Person B]

A few things to notice:

  • You are always "in cahoots with" someone. The word "with" is essential.
  • "Cahoots" is always plural. You would never say "in cahoot" — that sounds wrong and is never used.
  • It always needs at least two parties — you can't be "in cahoots" alone. It is, by definition, a group act.

"In cahoots" is almost always negative in tone. It carries a strong sense of suspicion, accusation, and moral disapproval.

When you say someone is "in cahoots" with another person, you are not simply saying they are working together. You are suggesting they are up to no good — that there is something corrupt, deceptive, or crooked about their collaboration.

Compare these two sentences:

  • "The two scientists are collaborating on a project." (neutral — no suspicion)
  • "The two scientists are in cahoots with the pharmaceutical company." (suspicious — implies something dishonest is going on)

Both sentences describe people working together, but "in cahoots" immediately signals that something is wrong.

However — and this is a small but important nuance — in very casual, light-hearted conversation between friends, people sometimes use "in cahoots" in a playful, non-serious way. For example, a parent might laugh and say, "I think the kids are in cahoots to stay up past their bedtime!" Here, it does not imply serious wrongdoing, just childish mischief. But this playful use is the exception, not the rule. In most real-world usage, the phrase carries genuine suspicion.

Here are examples that show how the phrase is naturally used:

  1. Politics & corruption:

"The investigation revealed that the mayor was in cahoots with the construction company, awarding them contracts in exchange for bribes."

  1. Crime:

"The store's security guard was in cahoots with the thieves, which is why they were never caught."

  1. Business fraud:

"Many investors believed the two firms were in cahoots to manipulate the stock price."

  1. Everyday suspicion:

"I think my brother and my mom are in cahoots — every time I get in trouble, she already knows about it before I even say anything."

  1. Playful / light use:

"Are you two in cahoots? You both showed up wearing the same shirt!"

The origin of "cahoots" is a little uncertain, but most language historians point to one likely source: the French word cahute, meaning a small cabin or hut. The image is of people huddled together in a small, hidden space — whispering, plotting, and conspiring away from others' eyes. That image of secrecy and closeness fits the meaning perfectly.

Another possible root is the French word cohorte (cohort), meaning a group of soldiers or companions — people united for a shared goal.

The word entered American English in the early 1800s, making it a distinctly American expression. It was especially common in the American South and West. By the mid-1800s, "in cahoots" was firmly established in everyday speech across the United States.

"In cahoots" is an informal, colloquial expression. You would hear it in:

  • Everyday conversation
  • Newspapers and journalism (especially in headlines or casual reporting)
  • Novels, films, and TV shows
  • Informal speeches or storytelling

You would not typically see it in:

  • Formal legal documents (where you'd use words like "conspiring" or "colluding")
  • Academic writing
  • Official government reports

That said, it is not slang — it is perfectly standard English, just on the casual side.
Words That Mean the Same Thing

If you want to express the same idea more formally, or simply vary your language, here are some alternatives:

  • Conspiring with — "He was conspiring with the enemy." (formal, strong)
  • Colluding with — "The companies were colluding to fix prices." (formal, used in business/legal contexts)
  • In league with — "She was in league with some very dangerous people." (semi-formal, slightly old-fashioned)
  • Hand in glove with — "The officials were hand in glove with the smugglers." (idiomatic, similar feel to "in cahoots")
  • Working in secret with — a plain, literal alternative

Among all of these, "in cahoots" is the most vivid and colorful, which is why it has survived in everyday English for over two centuries.
Quick Summary (The Essentials at a Glance)

• Meaning: Secretly working with someone, usually for a dishonest or sneaky purpose.
  • Structure: Always "in cahoots with someone."
  • Tone: Negative and suspicious (occasionally playful in casual speech).
  • Formality: Informal but standard English.
  • Origin: Likely from the French cahute (small hut) or cohorte (cohort); entered American English in the early 1800s.
  • Key traits of the situation it describes: Secrecy + at least two people + a questionable or dishonest goal.

When you hear "in cahoots," your brain should immediately picture a secret, shady alliance — two or more people quietly plotting together, keeping their partnership hidden because what they are doing would not look good in the open. That single image captures everything the idiom means.
8267:
"In camera" is a Latin phrase. In Latin, the word camera does not mean a photography device — it means a room or a chamber. So "in camera" literally translates to "in the room" or "in the chamber."

Interestingly, this is also where the photographic camera gets its name — early cameras were enclosed in a dark box called a camera obscura (Latin for "dark room"). So both the legal term and the photography device share the same Latin root, even though they have nothing to do with each other.
The Legal Meaning

In law, "in camera" means a legal proceeding — or part of one — that takes place in private, away from the public and the press.

Normally, court proceedings are open to everyone. Anyone can walk into a courtroom and watch a trial. This is called an open court hearing, and it is the default rule in most legal systems. The idea is that justice should be transparent — the public has a right to see how the courts operate.

But sometimes, a judge decides that a portion of the proceedings must be conducted privately, behind closed doors. That private proceeding is called an in camera proceeding (or "in camera hearing"). The general public, journalists, and spectators are asked to leave or are not allowed in at all.
Where Does the "Chamber" Come In?

The phrase originally referred to a judge's private chambers — the judge's personal office inside the courthouse. Historically, when something was handled "in camera," it literally happened inside that private room rather than in the open courtroom. Today, an in camera proceeding doesn't have to happen physically in the judge's office — it can happen in the courtroom itself with the public excluded — but the name has stuck.
Why Would a Court Go "In Camera"?

The core reason is to protect sensitive information or vulnerable people when the harm caused by a public hearing would outweigh the public's interest in watching.

Here are the most common reasons a judge orders an in camera proceeding:

1. Protecting children. When a child is a victim of abuse or a witness to a crime, a court may go in camera to spare the child the trauma of speaking in front of a crowd. Similarly, almost all juvenile (youth criminal) proceedings are conducted in camera to protect the minor's future.

2. National security and classified information. If a case involves state secrets, intelligence methods, or classified government documents, discussing these in an open courtroom would risk exposing them to the public — including to enemies. A judge will close the proceedings.

3. Trade secrets and confidential business information. A company's secret formula, customer lists, or proprietary technology might come up during a business dispute. Allowing that information to be heard publicly could destroy the company's competitive advantage. The court goes in camera to prevent this.

4. Sexual assault and privacy. In many places, when a rape or sexual assault case involves the victim's prior sexual history or deeply intimate details, courts close the proceedings to protect the victim's dignity and privacy, and to encourage victims to come forward without fear.

5. Witness protection. If a witness's identity or location must be kept secret to protect their safety, revealing it in open court would defeat the purpose.

6. Medical and psychological records. Sensitive personal health information that is relevant to a case may require the court to be cleared before it is discussed.
"In Camera Review" — A Special and Very Important Usage

Beyond full hearings, the term is also used in a more specific technical sense: in camera review.

Here is how it works: Imagine one party in a lawsuit claims that certain documents are privileged — meaning they are legally protected from being shown to the other side (for example, private communications between a lawyer and their client). The other party disputes this and wants those documents disclosed.

The judge is now in a bind. How can the judge decide whether the documents should be disclosed without first reading them? But if the judge reads them in open court, the confidentiality is already broken.

The solution: the judge privately reviews the documents alone, in camera, without either party present. After reading them in private, the judge decides whether they must be handed over or whether they stay protected. This is called an in camera review or in camera inspection.

In camera review is critically important because it allows a judge to act as a neutral gatekeeper — protecting sensitive material while still ensuring that parties cannot abuse the claim of privilege to hide evidence they are simply not entitled to hide.
Who Is Present During an In Camera Proceeding?

This depends on the type of proceeding and the reason for going in camera:

  • In a full in camera hearing, the public and press are excluded. Usually the judge, the parties (the people involved in the case), and their lawyers are still present.
  • In some cases — for example, where the sensitivity of the information is extreme — even one of the parties may be excluded, and only the judge and one side's lawyer are present. This is rarer and more controversial.
  • In an in camera review of documents, only the judge reviews the material. Nobody else is present for the review itself.
The Tension With the Right to a Public Trial

In many democratic legal systems (like the United States and the United Kingdom), there is a strong legal principle — sometimes even a constitutional or statutory right — that criminal trials must be held in public. This right exists for good reasons: it prevents secret courts, holds judges accountable, and allows society to see that justice is being done.

So when a court goes in camera, it is essentially making an exception to this important principle. Courts do not take this lightly. A judge must justify the decision to go in camera by showing that:

  1. There is a specific, serious reason to close the proceedings.
  2. Going in camera is necessary — there's no less restrictive way to protect the interest involved.
  3. The harm from keeping it open outweighs the public's interest in transparency.

Courts try to go in camera for only as much of the proceeding as necessary — not the whole trial if only one piece of evidence needs to be protected.
In Camera vs. "Sealed"

These two terms often appear together but mean slightly different things:

  • In camera refers to the proceedings themselves being private — people are excluded from the room.
  • Sealed refers to the records of those proceedings being kept confidential — the documents, transcripts, or evidence are not made publicly available.

An in camera proceeding is often also sealed (so that even the transcript is kept private), but not always. And sometimes records are sealed even without the proceeding being in camera.
In Camera vs. "In Chambers"

You will sometimes hear the phrase "in chambers" used in a similar way. While the two are related, there is a subtle difference:

  • In camera specifically means proceedings that are private because of sensitivity or confidentiality of the subject matter.
  • In chambers more broadly refers to informal meetings between the judge and the lawyers in the judge's private office — for example, to discuss scheduling, procedural matters, or minor legal arguments. These are not necessarily about sensitive evidence.

In practice, the two phrases sometimes overlap, and lawyers may use them loosely, but strict usage keeps them distinct.
How to Pronounce It
"In camera" is pronounced: "in KAM-er-a" — just as you would say the word "camera" in English, with "in" placed before it.
A Simple Summary to Anchor Everything

Think of it this way: courts, by default, do their work in public — like a theater with open doors. "In camera" is when the judge closes those doors. The reasons always come back to protecting something important: a child's innocence, a nation's secrets, a company's confidential information, or a victim's dignity. And when a judge reviews sensitive evidence alone before deciding whether to share it, that private review is also called "in camera." The common thread in every use of the term is privacy, protection, and the judge acting as a careful gatekeeper.
8268:
"In concert with" means working together with someone or something in a coordinated, unified way to achieve a shared goal or produce a combined result.

The simplest way to say it: doing something jointly, in a planned, cooperative manner.

"The health ministry worked in concert with hospitals to control the outbreak."

This means the health ministry and hospitals didn't just both happen to act — they coordinated with each other, planned together, and moved as a team.
The Secret Hidden Inside the Word "Concert"

To truly understand this idiom for life, you need to understand the word "concert" at its heart.

Most people know "concert" as a music performance — singers or musicians on stage. But why is a music show called a concert? Because the word "concert" originally comes from the Latin root "concertare," meaning to work together, to coordinate, to act as one unit. In a music concert, many musicians play different instruments, but they all follow the same rhythm, the same melody, the same conductor — they are in perfect coordination. That unity and harmony is the very soul of the word.

So when you say "in concert with," you are borrowing exactly that image: multiple parties moving like musicians in an orchestra — each doing their own part, but together, harmoniously, in coordination.

This is why the idiom feels so vivid once you understand its roots. It doesn't just mean "together." It means together in a deliberate, synchronized, cooperative way — the way musicians play together, not the way strangers accidentally walk in the same direction.
What Makes It Different From Just Saying "With" or "Together With"

This is a subtle but important point.

  • "She went to the store with her friend" — they went together. Simple fact. No strong sense of coordination or planning.
  • "She worked in concert with her friend to plan the event" — they coordinated, divided roles, and moved toward a shared goal as a team.

The phrase "in concert with" always carries the idea of intentional cooperation. There is a plan, a shared direction, and a joint effort. The parties involved are not just near each other — they are actively cooperating.

Think of it this way:

  • Two people accidentally wearing the same color shirt = together, but NOT "in concert with."
  • Two people planning and rehearsing a dance routine = working in concert with each other.
The Tone and Register — Who Uses It and Where

"In concert with" is a formal, sophisticated phrase. You will most commonly encounter it in:

  • News articles and journalism — "The central bank acted in concert with global financial institutions."
  • Legal and official documents — "The agency shall operate in concert with relevant authorities."
  • Business and corporate language — "The two firms launched the product in concert with their marketing teams."
  • Academic and scientific writing — "The immune system functions in concert with the nervous system."
  • Political and diplomatic speech — "The allied nations responded in concert with one another."

It is far less common in casual, everyday conversation. If you are chatting with a friend, you would say "we worked together" rather than "we acted in concert with each other." But in professional writing, formal speech, or any context that calls for precision and weight, "in concert with" fits perfectly and sounds highly intelligent.
The Three Things It Always Implies

Every single time "in concert with" is used correctly, it carries three built-in ideas:

1. Coordination — The parties involved have aligned their actions. They are not working at random. There is a shared plan or shared direction.

2. Cooperation — The parties are on the same side, working toward something together, not against each other.

3. Unified result — The combined effort produces something that a single party alone could not have produced as effectively, or the action is stronger because it is joint.

If any of these three ingredients is missing, the idiom is being used incorrectly.

Seeing an idiom in many different contexts is the best way to own it fully.

Politics:
"The prime minister, in concert with neighboring governments, announced a regional climate agreement."
→ Multiple governments coordinated together to produce a joint announcement.

Medicine/Science:
"The heart works in concert with the lungs to keep blood oxygenated."
→ Two organs coordinate their functions to achieve a shared biological outcome.

Business:
"The startup raised funds in concert with two venture capital firms."
→ They coordinated with the firms; it wasn't a solo effort.

Law enforcement:
"Local police, in concert with federal agencies, dismantled the smuggling network."
→ Two levels of law enforcement coordinated their resources and actions together.

Education:
"Teachers, in concert with parents, designed a new homework policy."
→ Both groups worked cooperatively; neither acted alone.

Military:
"The air force struck the target in concert with ground troops advancing from the south."
→ Two forces timed and coordinated their actions together for a unified military operation.

Notice that in every example, there are always at least two parties, and they are always actively cooperating toward something.
Synonyms — And How They Differ Slightly

These phrases are close in meaning, but each has a small shade of difference:

"In conjunction with" — Very similar to "in concert with," but it can sometimes just mean "alongside" or "combined with" without necessarily implying active cooperation. For example, "take this pill in conjunction with food" doesn't mean the pill and food are cooperating — they are just used together. "In concert with" always implies active coordination between parties that can make choices.

"In collaboration with" — Also very close, but this leans more toward creative or intellectual joint work — co-writing a book, co-designing a product, co-researching a topic. "In concert with" is broader and can apply to any coordinated action, not just creative ones.

"In partnership with" — Emphasizes a formal or ongoing relationship between the parties, often in business or institutional contexts. "In concert with" can describe a one-time coordinated effort, while "in partnership with" suggests something more ongoing.

"Together with" — The most casual and simplest of the group. No special implication of planning or coordination. "In concert with" is the more formal and precise choice when the coordination is the important point.

"Jointly with" — Very similar to "in concert with" but slightly more neutral and legal in feel. Used often in legal and official contexts.

Do not use "in concert with" to describe things that are merely happening at the same time but are NOT coordinating with each other.

❌ "It rained in concert with the football game." — Rain and a football game are not coordinating. They just happened simultaneously. This is wrong.

✅ "The fire department, in concert with city volunteers, controlled the blaze." — Two groups actively coordinating. This is correct.

The key test: Can the parties involved actually choose to cooperate? If yes, "in concert with" works. If you're just describing two things happening at the same time with no active coordination between them, choose a different phrase like "simultaneously with" or "alongside."
A Memory Hook That Will Stay With You Forever

Picture a symphony orchestra. Dozens of musicians, each with a different instrument. The violins, the cellos, the trumpets, the drums — all different, all separate. But when the conductor raises the baton, they all move together in perfect harmony, reading the same score, following the same beat, producing a unified masterpiece.

That image IS the idiom.

Whenever you see or hear "in concert with," just picture that orchestra. Multiple parties. One shared direction. Perfect coordination. Working as one.

"In concert with" means working in deliberate, coordinated cooperation with one or more other parties toward a shared goal — borrowed from the image of musicians performing together in harmony, and used primarily in formal, professional contexts to describe joint, unified action.
8269:
When someone is "in dire straits," they are in a very serious, dangerous, or desperate situation — one where things have gone badly wrong and the options available to fix it are very few or very difficult. The situation is urgent and threatening, not just mildly inconvenient.

Think of it like being stuck in a deep hole. You didn't just trip — you fell far down, the walls are steep, and climbing out won't be easy.

Examples of the idea:

  • A person who has lost their job, has no savings, and can't pay rent is in dire straits.
  • A country that is running out of food, medicine, and money is in dire straits.
  • A company about to go bankrupt with no investors willing to help is in dire straits.

The phrase always signals something serious and urgent — not everyday stress, but genuine, pressing hardship.

To truly understand this phrase, let's look at each word separately, because they are both a little unusual.

1. "Dire"

"Dire" is an adjective that means extremely serious, terrible, or dreadful. It emphasizes that something is not just bad — it is urgently bad, almost frighteningly so.

You can also hear it in other common expressions:

  • "Dire consequences" — very serious or devastating results
  • "Dire warning" — a very strong warning about something terrible
  • "Dire need" — an urgent, desperate need

So whenever you see "dire," think: this is extremely serious, not just a little bad.

2. "Straits"

This is the trickier word. "Straits" (often used in the plural) has two meanings — one geographical and one figurative — and both are important for understanding the idiom.

The geographical meaning: A "strait" (singular) is a narrow strip of water that connects two larger bodies of water. Famous real-world examples include:

  • The Strait of Gibraltar (the narrow waterway between Spain and Morocco connecting the Atlantic Ocean to the Mediterranean Sea)
  • The Strait of Hormuz (between Iran and Oman, connecting the Persian Gulf to the Arabian Sea)

These waterways are tight and narrow. Ships passing through them have very little room to maneuver. One wrong move and disaster strikes.

The figurative meaning: Because a strait is so narrow and confining, the word began to be used to describe difficult or tight situations in life — situations where you feel hemmed in, with very little room to move or act freely. If you are in "straits," you are in a situation with very few options, just like a ship in a tight, narrow channel.

The word "strait" in this figurative sense is ancient in the English language. You can even find it in the Bible — in Matthew 7:14, the phrase "strait gate" refers to a narrow, difficult path (this is also where the expression "straight and narrow" partly comes from, though that is a different phrase).

So putting it together: "dire straits" = a situation so tight and narrow (straits) that it is extremely threatening and serious (dire). You are trapped, squeezed, with barely any room or option to escape.

The word "dire" comes from the Latin word dirus, meaning fearful, ominous, or threatening. Romans used it to describe terrible omens and dreadful events.

The word "strait" comes from the Latin strictus, meaning tight or drawn together — which is also where we get the English words "strict" and "strict." It entered English through Old French (estreit, meaning narrow). You can see the connection: a strict rule tightens your behavior, and a strait tightens the space around you.

The combination of "dire" and "straits" in the figurative sense has been used in English for several centuries, though it became especially popular in modern usage. The idea of being in a dangerously tight spot — with no easy way out — made the phrase extremely versatile and it stuck.
How It Is Used in Sentences

"In dire straits" almost always follows the verb "to be" (is, are, was, were, etc.) or verbs like "find oneself" or "leave someone."

Basic structure:

Someone/something + is/are/was + in dire straits.

Examples:

  • "After the hurricane destroyed their home, the family was in dire straits."
  • "The hospital is in dire straits — it has no funding, no supplies, and not enough staff."
  • "He lost all his money gambling and found himself in dire straits."
  • "Years of mismanagement left the company in dire straits."
  • "If we don't get help soon, we'll be in dire straits."

Notice that the phrase works for people, organizations, countries, economies — any entity that can be in trouble.
The Tone and Register of the Phrase

"In dire straits" is slightly formal but widely understood. You will find it in:

  • Newspaper and magazine articles
  • News broadcasts
  • Serious conversations
  • Formal writing and essays

You would not typically use it in very casual small talk (e.g., "I'm in dire straits because I can't find my socks"), because the phrase carries a weight and seriousness to it. It implies real, significant trouble — not minor annoyances.

That said, people sometimes use it with humor or exaggeration in informal settings to describe a mildly bad situation for comic effect. Context will always make it clear whether it is serious or playful.

A few things to be clear about:

  • It does not refer to a geographical strait. When you hear this phrase in everyday speech, it is always the figurative, idiomatic meaning. Nobody says "in dire straits" to describe a narrow waterway being in bad shape.
  • It does not mean "just difficult." Being "in dire straits" is not the same as having a hard day or a tough week. The situation must be seriously threatening — financial ruin, grave danger, extreme hardship.
  • "Straits" is not the same as "straight." A very common mistake is to spell or write it as "in dire straights." That is incorrect. The word is "straits" — from the geographical and old English word meaning a narrow, tight passage — not "straight" as in a straight line.

If you hear any of these, they carry a similar meaning to "in dire straits":

  • "In a tight spot" — in a difficult situation with few options
  • "In deep trouble" — in serious difficulty
  • "In hot water" — in a problematic or dangerous situation
  • "Up against it" — facing very difficult circumstances
  • "In a bind" — stuck in a hard situation
  • "At the end of one's rope" — with no options or energy left
  • "In desperate circumstances" — facing an urgent, serious crisis

Among all of these, "in dire straits" tends to sound the most formal and carries the strongest sense of genuine urgency and severity.

You may have heard of the British rock band called Dire Straits, famous for songs like "Sultans of Swing" and "Money for Nothing." They were active from the late 1970s through the 1990s. The band chose their name directly from this idiom — they were struggling, broke musicians when they started out, and the phrase captured their situation perfectly. This is a great memory trick: if you ever forget what the phrase means, just picture a band of young, broke, struggling musicians trying to make it — that's exactly the image the phrase conveys.

MeaningIn a very serious, dangerous, or desperate situation with few options
ToneSerious and urgent — not used for minor problems
Key word "dire"Extremely serious, terrible, threatening
Key word "straits"Figuratively: a tight, confined situation with little room to act
Common mistakeWriting "straights" instead of "straits"
RegisterSlightly formal, but widely understood

In short: if someone or something is "in dire straits," they are in deep, serious trouble — trapped in a difficult situation, under real pressure, and urgently needing help or a way out.
8270:
When you do something in earnest, you do it seriously, sincerely, and with real effort and determination — not as a joke, not halfheartedly, and not just to pretend.

Think of it as the opposite of "playing around." If you're in earnest, you genuinely mean what you say or you're fully committed to what you're doing.

This idiom carries two closely related but slightly different shades of meaning. Understanding both is key.

1. Sincerely — "I truly mean this"

Here, "in earnest" tells you that a person is being completely genuine — not joking, not exaggerating, not being sarcastic.

"I'm asking you in earnest — please don't leave."

This means: I am 100% serious. This is not a joke. I genuinely mean this.

"She said it in earnest, but everyone thought she was teasing."

This means: She was being completely sincere, even though others didn't realize it.

In this sense, "in earnest" answers the question: "Are you serious or just messing around?" — and the answer is: serious.

2. With Full Force / Intensity — "Things are really getting going now"

Here, "in earnest" describes an activity that has truly begun, picked up full speed, or is now being done with maximum energy. It often suggests that something was slow, light, or tentative before — but now it's happening for real and with full power.

"The rain started in earnest around midnight."

This means: There may have been a few light drops before, but now it's really raining hard.

"After months of delays, construction finally began in earnest."

This means: Work has now truly started and is moving with full effort and commitment.

"She studied in earnest for the first time after failing the exam."

This means: She put in real, serious, determined effort — not the casual studying she did before.

In this sense, "in earnest" answers the question: "Is this really happening fully yet?" — and the answer is: yes, now it truly is.
How the Two Meanings Are Related

You might wonder — are these really the same idiom? Yes, and here's why they feel connected:

Both meanings share a common thread: authenticity and full commitment.

  • Being sincere = your words are authentic, not fake.
  • Doing something with full effort = your action is authentic, not half-done.

In both cases, you're going all the way. There's no holding back, no pretending, no going through the motions. Whether it's a feeling, a statement, or an activity — "in earnest" means it's the real deal.
Where Does the Word "Earnest" Come From?

The word earnest (on its own) is an adjective that means serious, sincere, and deeply committed. It comes from the Old English word eornost, which meant seriousness or zeal.

So when you say "in earnest," you're literally saying "in a state of seriousness." Over many centuries, this became a fixed idiom that people use without thinking about the individual words anymore.

Note: There is also a noun "earnest" (as in "a deposit or pledge"), but that's a completely different word with different origins. Don't confuse the two. The idiom "in earnest" comes from the adjective earnest, not the noun.

"In earnest" is an adverbial phrase — meaning it describes how something is done, not a person or a thing. It usually sits:

After the verb:

"He spoke in earnest."
"The project started in earnest."

At the end of a sentence:

"This time, she meant it in earnest."

Occasionally at the beginning for emphasis:

"In earnest, I believe this is the right decision." (Less common, more formal.)

"In earnest" often carries an emotional undercurrent. When someone does something in earnest, it frequently implies:

  • Urgency — this matters to them deeply.
  • Contrast — there was a "before" (casual, joking, slow) and now this is the serious "after."
  • Vulnerability — being sincere means opening yourself up genuinely.

This is why the phrase can feel moving or even touching in context. If someone says "I'm telling you this in earnest", you understand that they're not playing games — they're putting their true self forward.
Common Words and Phrases That Go with "In Earnest"

Certain words appear beside "in earnest" very often. Recognizing these patterns will help you feel natural using the phrase:

  • begin / start in earnest — the most common combo; describes when something truly gets underway.
  • mean it in earnest — to say something genuinely, without irony.
  • say / speak in earnest — to communicate sincerely.
  • work in earnest — to apply real, dedicated effort.
  • search in earnest — to look for something with real determination.

Clearing up what this idiom does not mean will sharpen your understanding:

  • It does not mean "eagerly" or "excitedly" — you can be in earnest while being calm and quiet.
  • It does not mean "quickly" — doing something in earnest is about sincerity and effort, not speed (though speed may follow naturally).
  • It does not mean "angrily" or "seriously" in the sense of being stern or cold. A person can say something warmly and lovingly in earnest.

—ExampleWhat It Means
🗣️"I'm joking... or am I? No, I'm asking in earnest."I'm genuinely asking, not joking.
🌧️"The storm hit in earnest after sunset."The storm truly arrived with full power.
📚"He only began studying in earnest two weeks before the exam."He only started putting in real, serious effort then.
❤️"She said 'I love you' in earnest for the first time."She said it genuinely, from the heart.
🏗️"Negotiations began in earnest after the ceasefire."Real, serious, committed negotiations finally started.
One Sentence to Remember It Forever

If you want just one mental anchor for this idiom, remember this:

"In earnest" = for real, with full heart and full effort.

Anytime you see or hear it, ask yourself: "Is this the 'for real, fully committed' version of something?" — and almost always, the answer will be yes.
8271:
