Very often, it gently pushes back against a wrong belief, a misunderstanding, or an assumption. It implies: "What you think may be wrong, but here is the truth."

Here are examples that show the idiom in action. Notice how it always introduces a truth, often one that surprises or corrects something.

Example 1 — Correcting a wrong belief:

"Everyone thinks this building is 100 years old. In point of fact, it was built only 40 years ago."

(The truth corrects a common assumption.)

Example 2 — Emphasizing a surprising truth:

"She looks very calm. In point of fact, she is extremely nervous inside."

(The real situation is the opposite of what appears on the surface.)

Example 3 — Adding an important true detail:

"He said the trip would be cheap. In point of fact, it cost us a fortune."

(The real outcome contradicts what was promised.)

Example 4 — Strengthening a claim:

"This is not just a good book. In point of fact, it is one of the greatest novels ever written."

(Here, there is no correction — the speaker is simply using the idiom to add strong emphasis to a true statement.)
How It Feels in a Sentence

When you hear or read "in point of fact," it creates a specific feeling or tone. It sounds:

  • Formal and serious — It is not casual language. It suits writing, speeches, debates, and professional conversations far more than it suits everyday chat with friends.
  • Authoritative — The speaker sounds confident and knowledgeable, like someone who really knows the truth of the matter.
  • Slightly corrective — Even when it is not directly correcting someone, it carries a quiet sense of "let me clarify the reality here."
Where It Sits in a Sentence

"In point of fact" almost always appears at the beginning of a sentence or clause, and it is followed by a comma.

In point of fact, the Earth is not perfectly round — it is slightly flattened at the poles.

You can also place it in the middle of a sentence, between two commas, to add emphasis mid-thought:

The evidence, in point of fact, points strongly in the other direction.

Placing it at the very end of a sentence is rare and generally sounds awkward, so it is best to avoid that.
How It Compares to Similar Expressions

There are several expressions with nearly the same meaning. Understanding how they differ helps you use each one correctly.

"In fact" — This is the shorter, more common, and less formal sibling of "in point of fact." Both mean the same thing, but "in point of fact" sounds much more deliberate and emphatic. Use "in fact" in everyday writing; use "in point of fact" when you want a more formal, weighty tone.

"As a matter of fact" — Almost identical in meaning. This one is slightly more conversational than "in point of fact" but still formal enough for professional use.

"Actually" — The most casual of the group. It carries the same core idea but is used in everyday speech. "Actually, he never said that" feels natural in a friendly conversation, whereas "In point of fact, he never said that" would feel more like a formal debate or a legal discussion.

"In reality" — Very close in meaning, and often interchangeable. "In reality" places a slightly stronger emphasis on the contrast between what seems to be true and what actually is true.

"Indeed" — This one is used more for confirming something rather than correcting it. It adds strength and agreement rather than contrast.

This phrase has roots in legal and formal English, where precision matters enormously. In law, a "point of fact" refers to a specific question about what actually happened — as opposed to a "point of law," which refers to how the law should be interpreted. Over centuries, "in point of fact" moved beyond courtrooms and into general formal usage, where it came to simply mean "in reality" or "actually."

It has been used in written English since at least the 17th and 18th centuries and is found throughout classical literature, formal essays, and scholarly writing.
When to Use It and When Not To

Use it when:

  • You are writing a formal essay, report, or article.
  • You are in a professional discussion, debate, or presentation.
  • You want to correct a misunderstanding with authority and precision.
  • You want to add strong, serious emphasis to a true statement.

Avoid it when:

  • You are having a casual conversation with friends or family. It would sound stiff and out of place.
  • You are writing a text message or social media post. "Actually" or "in fact" would feel far more natural.
One-Line Summary to Remember It Forever

"In point of fact" = "The truth is…" — used in formal situations to state reality clearly, often to correct what is wrong or to emphasize what is true.

Once you understand that this idiom is simply a formal, emphatic way of saying "actually" or "the truth is," you will recognize it instantly everywhere — in books, speeches, news articles, and academic writing — and use it with full confidence whenever the moment calls for it.
8284:
"In short order" means very quickly, without delay, and without wasting any time.

When someone does something in short order, they do it fast, efficiently, and without a lot of fuss or waiting around.

Think of it like this: Imagine you ask a very skilled chef to make you a sandwich. Within two minutes, it's done perfectly and sitting in front of you. That chef made your sandwich in short order.

This idiom can feel a little confusing at first because the words don't seem to obviously add up to the meaning. Let's look at them:

  • "Short" here refers to a short amount of time — not a short length or a short person, but brevity in time.
  • "Order" here means a command or instruction — like when a boss gives an order, or a customer places an order at a restaurant.

So "in short order" essentially means "within a short time of receiving the command/instruction." Over time, the phrase became a fixed idiom used simply to mean quickly and efficiently.

This phrase has its roots in American military language, dating back to the mid-1800s.

In the military, soldiers are given orders — commands they must follow. To carry out an order in short order meant to execute it swiftly and without hesitation, exactly as a disciplined soldier should. There was no dawdling, no delay — just immediate, efficient action.

Over time, this military expression spread into everyday civilian language, and people began using it outside of warfare — in workplaces, homes, sports, and daily life — to simply mean quickly.

Some people also connect this idiom to short-order cooking — the style of fast cooking done at diners and cafes where food is made quickly on demand. A short-order cook doesn't take 45 minutes to make your breakfast; your eggs are in front of you fast. This connection strengthened the idiom's association with speed and efficiency in people's minds.

"In short order" is an adverbial phrase. This means it describes how an action is done — in this case, it tells you the speed at which something happens.

It most commonly appears at the end of a sentence:

  • "She finished the entire report in short order."
  • "The technician fixed the computer in short order."

It can also appear at the beginning of a sentence:

  • "In short order, the rescue team found the missing hikers."
  • "In short order, she cleaned the entire house."

It pairs with action verbs — things that get done. You'll almost always see it after verbs like finished, solved, completed, handled, settled, fixed, built, learned, etc.

Here are examples to show how naturally this idiom fits into different areas of life:

Work / Professional:
"The new manager identified the company's problems and fixed them in short order."
(She didn't take months — she sorted things out quickly.)

Cooking / Daily life:
"He prepared a full three-course meal in short order."
(He was fast and efficient in the kitchen.)

Learning / School:
"Once the concept clicked, she solved all the remaining problems in short order."
(After understanding it, she flew through the rest quickly.)

Sports:
"The champion defeated his opponent in short order."
(It wasn't a long, drawn-out fight — it was over fast.)

Problem-solving:
"The experienced plumber diagnosed the leak and repaired it in short order."
(No wasted time — he got it done quickly.)
The Subtle Feeling the Idiom Carries

This is important: "In short order" doesn't just mean fast. It carries a slightly extra flavor that plain words like "quickly" or "fast" don't fully capture. It suggests:

  1. Efficiency — not just speed, but effective speed. The job was done well and quickly.
  2. Decisiveness — there was no hesitating, no second-guessing, no wasted motion.
  3. A mild sense of impressiveness — when you say something was done in short order, there's often a quiet sense of admiration for how cleanly and quickly it was handled.

Compare these two sentences:

  • "He quickly fixed the engine."
  • "He fixed the engine in short order."

Both mean fast, but the second one feels more complete — it paints a picture of someone competent, confident, and unhesitating. That's the extra layer "in short order" adds.

To be absolutely clear, here are things this idiom does not mean:

  • It does not mean in a short line or in a queue.
  • It does not mean briefly (as in a short speech or short explanation).
  • It does not refer to small or short things in size.
  • The word "short" here is purely about time, not anything physical.
Words and Phrases That Mean Something Similar

If you ever want to express the same idea with different words, here are close alternatives:

  • Quickly / swiftly / rapidly
  • Without delay
  • Promptly
  • In no time / in no time at all
  • Right away
  • Before long
  • Efficiently and fast

That said, none of these carry the exact same sharp, slightly formal, and efficient tone that "in short order" does. It has its own personality.

"In short order" sits comfortably in both formal and informal settings. You can use it in:

  • A business report or professional email ✓
  • A casual conversation with a friend ✓
  • A newspaper article or news broadcast ✓
  • A novel or a story ✓

It is slightly more common in American English than in British English, though speakers of both understand it perfectly well.
One-Line Summary to Remember It Forever

"In short order" = done quickly, efficiently, and without wasting any time — often implying skill and decisiveness.

Whenever you see or hear this phrase, picture that skilled chef again — calm, confident, and placing a perfectly made sandwich in front of you within two minutes. That's "in short order" in action.
8285:
"In situ" means in the original place — right there, where something already is, without moving it or taking it somewhere else.

When something is done in situ, it is done at the exact location where the thing naturally exists or was originally found. Nothing is removed, relocated, or transported. The action happens on the spot, in place.
The Single Idea That Holds Everything Together

The entire meaning of in situ revolves around one central idea: no relocation.

Imagine a broken pipe inside a wall. A plumber could either tear out the pipe, take it to the workshop, fix it there, and bring it back — or fix it right there inside the wall, without removing it. When the plumber fixes it right there, that is working in situ. The pipe never leaves its place. The work comes to the object, not the other way around.

This is the spirit of the word: you go to the thing; the thing doesn't come to you.
How It Works as an Adverb

As an adverb, in situ tells you where or in what manner an action takes place. It modifies a verb by saying the action happened at the original location of the subject.

Here are some examples:

  • "The engineers repaired the bridge in situ." — They repaired it while it was still standing. They didn't dismantle it and haul pieces to a factory.
  • "The scientist examined the rock formation in situ." — She studied it right there in the landscape, not after chipping it off and taking it to a lab.
  • "The tumor was treated in situ." — The treatment was applied right inside the body, at the exact spot of the tumor.

Notice that in every case, the phrase is answering the question: where was the action performed? Answer: right there, in its place.
Where You Will Encounter This Word

In situ appears across many fields, and knowing its core meaning will help you understand it in all of them.

In medicine and biology, a cancer described as in situ is one that has stayed exactly where it started — it has not spread to other tissues or organs. It is contained, still in its original location. This is why "carcinoma in situ" is considered an early, localized stage — the cancer hasn't traveled anywhere yet.

In archaeology, when a relic or artifact is found in situ, it means it is still lying in the exact spot where it was originally left, used, or buried — perhaps thousands of years ago. This is enormously significant to archaeologists because an undisturbed artifact tells a far richer story about the past than one that has been moved or disturbed. Finding pottery in situ in a kitchen tells you it was used there; the same pottery found moved elsewhere tells you much less.

In science and environmental work, researchers often prefer to study or measure things in situ — meaning in their natural environment, in real conditions — rather than collecting samples and studying them in a lab. A water quality sensor dropped into a river measures in situ; collecting river water in a bottle and testing it back in a lab is the opposite.

In engineering and construction, repairs or tests done in situ are done on-site, within the structure itself, without dismantling. Concrete poured directly into a mold at the construction site hardens in situ; prefabricated concrete made at a factory and transported is not.
The Nuance: Original Context, Not Just Location

Here is a subtler point that separates in situ from simply meaning "on-site" or "nearby."

In situ doesn't just mean somewhere at the location — it specifically means in the original, undisturbed position or context. The emphasis is on things being where they naturally or originally belong.

For example: if archaeologists move an artifact just a few meters away from where they dug it up — even if they're still at the same dig site — that artifact is no longer in situ. It has been displaced from its original position, and that displacement matters.

This is why the phrase carries weight in scientific and academic settings. It signals authenticity of place — the assurance that something hasn't been tampered with, relocated, or taken out of its natural context.

There is no single standard antonym for in situ, but the opposite idea is sometimes expressed as doing something ex situ (meaning "out of place" or "off-site"). More commonly, the contrast is just described plainly: removing something to study or fix it elsewhere.

  • In situ treatment of contaminated soil = cleaning the polluted soil right where it sits in the ground.
  • Ex situ / opposite approach = digging up the contaminated soil, trucking it to a treatment facility, processing it there.

Understanding this contrast will sharpen your sense of the word enormously. Whenever you see in situ, ask yourself: Is this thing being dealt with right where it lives, without being uprooted? If yes, the word fits perfectly.

In situ as an adverb means in the original place, without moving or removing the subject. It describes an action — a study, a repair, a treatment, an observation — that happens right where the subject naturally is. The word is used widely in science, medicine, archaeology, and engineering, but its meaning never changes: the work comes to the thing; the thing stays put.
8286:
When you are "in someone's bad books," it means that person is unhappy, disappointed, or angry with you. They have a negative opinion of you right now, usually because of something you said or did (or forgot to do).

Think of it this way: imagine a person carrying an invisible notebook. In that notebook, they write the names of people they are pleased with on one page, and the names of people who have upset or disappointed them on another page. If your name ends up on the bad page, you are in their bad books.

It is a way of saying: "That person is not happy with me."
Simple Examples to Make It Crystal Clear

• "I forgot to call my mum on her birthday. Now I'm in her bad books."
    Your mother is upset with you.
  • "Don't submit your work late again, or you'll be in the manager's bad books."
    The manager will be displeased with you.
  • "He broke his friend's favourite mug and didn't apologise. He's been in his friend's bad books ever since."
    His friend is still angry with him.

Notice the pattern: something happened → someone got upset → that person is now in someone's bad books.
Where Does This Phrase Come From?

The phrase is rooted in a very real, historical practice. Centuries ago — particularly in medieval Europe — monasteries, institutions, and merchants kept actual written books or ledgers. These books were used to record important information about people: who behaved well, who owed money, who had broken a rule or caused trouble.

If your name was recorded in the section for wrongdoers or troublemakers, you were quite literally in the bad book. Over time, this very specific, physical idea became a figurative expression — meaning, it stopped referring to a real book and started being used loosely to describe any situation where someone is displeased with another person.

Eventually, the phrase evolved into the plural "bad books," which is the form we use today.
The Opposite Phrase: "In Someone's Good Books"

Every phrase like this has an opposite, and this one is wonderfully simple:

"In someone's good books" means the opposite — that person thinks well of you, is pleased with you, or approves of you.

  • "I stayed late to help my boss finish the project. I think I'm in her good books now."
    The boss is pleased with you.

So you can think of it like a scale:

  • Good books = that person likes what you've done ✅
  • Bad books = that person is unhappy with you ❌
How Is It Used in a Sentence? (Grammar Guide)

The phrase always follows this structure:

[Subject] + [be verb] + in + [person's] + bad books

Here are the different ways it can appear in tenses:

  • Present: "I am in her bad books." / "I'm in her bad books."
  • Past: "He was in the teacher's bad books all term."
  • Future: "If you do that, you'll be in their bad books."
  • Present Perfect: "She's been in his bad books since the argument last week."

You can also use it as a warning:

  • "Watch out — don't be in his bad books."
  • "Try not to get into the boss's bad books."
The Tone and Feel of This Phrase

This is an informal, conversational phrase. You would use it in everyday speech or casual writing — not in a formal essay or official document.

It has a slightly light-hearted tone, even though the situation it describes (someone being angry or disappointed with you) is not always pleasant. Native speakers sometimes use it with a touch of humour.

It is particularly popular in British English, but it is widely understood across all English-speaking countries.
Synonyms — Other Ways to Say the Same Thing

If you want to express the same idea with different words, here are some alternatives:

  • "In the doghouse" — very informal, same idea; someone is in trouble with another person.
  • "Out of favour" — slightly more formal; someone no longer has the approval of another.
  • "On someone's bad side" — you have made someone feel negatively toward you.
  • "In trouble with someone" — simple and direct.

All of these carry roughly the same meaning, but "in someone's bad books" has a unique charm because of its vivid, old-fashioned imagery of a literal book.
How Do You Get OUT of Someone's Bad Books?

This is a natural question! When you're in someone's bad books, you usually need to:

  1. Apologise sincerely for what you did.
  2. Make it right — fix the mistake or make amends.
  3. Give it time — sometimes, people need space to cool down.
  4. Show through actions (not just words) that you have changed or learned.

Once the person forgives you or approves of you again, you could say: "I'm back in her good books."

The phraseIn someone's bad books
Core meaningSomeone is displeased, disappointed, or angry with you
ToneInformal, conversational, slightly light-hearted
OriginReal historical books/ledgers used to record wrongdoers
OppositeIn someone's good books
Common inBritish English (understood everywhere)

The beauty of this phrase is its simplicity: it paints a clear picture — someone has written your name on the "bad" page of their invisible notebook, and you need to earn your way back to the "good" page. Once you understand that image, the phrase will never confuse you again.
8287:
When you are "in someone's good books," it means that person likes you, approves of you, or thinks highly of you at a particular moment. You have their respect, goodwill, or positive regard.

Think of it this way: imagine a person who matters to you — your boss, your teacher, your parent, or your neighbor. If that person is happy with you, trusts you, and sees you in a positive light, then you are in their good books.

It is that simple. The phrase is just a colorful way of saying "this person is pleased with me."
Where Did This Phrase Come From?

The phrase has a fascinating history rooted in a very old, very literal practice.

Centuries ago — especially in medieval Europe — people in positions of authority (merchants, lords, employers, monks) would keep written ledgers and record books. These were physical books where they tracked important information about the people around them: who was trustworthy, who had done good work, who owed them something, and who had behaved badly.

If your name was noted positively in such a book, it meant you were in good standing — quite literally, in their "good books." If your name was marked negatively, you were in their "bad books."

Over time, as people stopped keeping literal books for this purpose, the phrases survived as idioms — fixed expressions that carry a meaning beyond their literal words. So today, even though no one is actually writing your name in a physical book, the expression still captures the idea of being viewed favorably by someone.

There is also a connection to religious tradition. The Christian concept of the "Book of Life" — a divine record in which the names of the righteous and the favored are written — reinforced the idea that being "in someone's books" meant you had earned a good place in their eyes.
Breaking Down the Phrase Word by Word

Sometimes understanding each part of an idiom helps it stick better.

  • "In" — suggests you occupy a position, a status, or a place (in this case, a symbolic one).
  • "Someone's" — this can be anyone: your teacher, your parent, your employer, your friend, a neighbor, even a community.
  • "Good books" — the symbolic record of people who are viewed favorably by that person.

Put it together: you occupy a favorable position in the way someone views and thinks about you.
How Is It Used in Sentences?

Here are clear, practical examples that show you the phrase in real life:

Basic use:

"I finished all my work early this week, so I'm in my manager's good books right now."

(The manager is pleased with the person.)

Talking about another person:

"Priya always helps the professor after class. She's definitely in his good books."

(The professor likes and approves of Priya.)

Talking about an effort to gain someone's favor:

"I baked a cake for my neighbor to get back in her good books after my dog dug up her garden."

(The speaker is trying to regain the neighbor's positive opinion.)

A warning or advice:

"Don't forget her birthday if you want to stay in her good books."

(A reminder to keep someone's goodwill.)

The phrase has a small family of closely related expressions you should know.

1. "In someone's bad books"

This is the direct opposite. If you are in someone's bad books, they are displeased with you, they distrust you, or they hold a negative opinion of you.

"I came home two hours late without calling. Now I'm in my mother's bad books."

2. "Get into someone's good books"

This means to deliberately do something to earn someone's positive regard — to work your way into their favor.

"He volunteered to stay after hours to get into his boss's good books."

3. "Stay in someone's good books"

This means to maintain the positive opinion someone already has of you — to not ruin the goodwill you've built.

"She always delivers her assignments on time to stay in her professor's good books."

4. "Fall out of someone's good books"

This means to lose someone's favor — to go from being liked or trusted to being viewed negatively.

"He fell out of his client's good books after missing three deadlines."

5. "In someone's black book" (British English)

Slightly different in nuance — a "black book" traditionally refers to a private list someone keeps of people they want to avoid, punish, or distrust. Being in someone's black book suggests a more serious or lasting negative standing.
Similar Expressions That Mean the Same Thing

Knowing synonymous phrases helps you understand and recognize the meaning in different contexts:

  • "In someone's favor" — She is in the director's favor after that brilliant presentation.
  • "On someone's good side" — Always try to stay on your landlord's good side.
  • "In someone's good graces" — He worked hard to get back in his grandmother's good graces.
  • "Well-regarded by someone" — She is well-regarded by her entire team.

All of these carry the same core meaning: a person thinks positively of you.
Register and Tone — When and Where Is It Used?

This phrase is informal and conversational. You would use it naturally when talking with friends, family, or colleagues in everyday situations. You would not typically use it in a very formal essay or an official report — in those settings, you would say something like "viewed favorably by" or "held in high regard by."

It is widely used in British English and is well understood across other varieties of English too, including American and Australian English.
A Simple Way to Remember It Forever

Picture this in your mind:

A strict but fair teacher keeps an old-fashioned notebook on her desk. In that notebook, she writes the names of students she is proud of on one side — the good pages — and students she is disappointed in on the other side — the bad pages. If your name is on the good pages, you are in her good books. If it's on the bad pages, you are in her bad books.

Now whenever you hear this idiom, that mental image will anchor the meaning instantly.

Core meaningSomeone likes, approves of, or thinks highly of you
OppositeIn someone's bad books (they dislike or disapprove of you)
ToneInformal, conversational
OriginLiteral record-keeping books used to note people in good or bad standing

To put it in one sentence: if you are "in someone's good books," that person is happy with you and views you positively — and you would do well to stay there.
8288:
"In someone's/something's stead" means "in the place of someone/something" — acting as a substitute or replacement for them.

When you do something in someone's stead, you are doing what that person was supposed to do, because they cannot (or will not) do it themselves.

The whole idiom rests on one old, mostly forgotten word: stead.

"Stead" is an ancient English word meaning "place" or "position." It is rarely used on its own in modern English, but it lives on quietly inside several familiar words:

  • Instead — this is literally "in stead," meaning "in (its) place." When you say "I'll have tea instead of coffee," you're saying tea will take the place of coffee.
  • Homestead — the place of one's home.
  • Steadfast — literally "fixed in place," meaning firm and unwavering.

So "in someone's stead" is just the older, more formal version of saying "in someone's place."

The idiom follows a simple pattern:

[verb] + in + [person's/thing's] + stead

The verb is usually something like go, act, serve, speak, attend, appear, come, write.

1. With a person:

"The king was gravely ill, so his eldest son attended the royal banquet in his stead."

Here, the son went to the banquet in place of the king — he filled the king's role because the king could not be there.

"She was stuck abroad, so she asked her colleague to accept the award in her stead."

The colleague received the award on her behalf, as her substitute.

"I cannot fight in this war. Will you go in my stead?"

"Will you go where I was supposed to go, and do what I was supposed to do?"

2. With a thing:

"The old wooden bridge was torn down, and a stronger steel one was built in its stead."

The steel bridge replaced the wooden one — it stands in the place of the old bridge.

"The harsh punishment was abolished, and a fairer system was introduced in its stead."

The fairer system took the place of the old punishment.

This idiom is formal and literary. You would find it in:

  • Novels, especially historical fiction or classic literature
  • Formal speeches or ceremonies
  • Legal or official documents
  • Religious texts

You would not typically hear it in casual everyday conversation. In day-to-day speech, people simply say "instead of him," "in his place," "on her behalf," or "as a replacement." But in writing — especially when you want a slightly elevated or dignified tone — "in someone's stead" is a precise and elegant choice.

What makes this phrase special is the weight of the role, not just the physical presence.

When someone acts in your stead, they don't merely show up where you would have shown up. They take on your function, duty, or responsibility in that situation. The idea is one of genuine substitution — stepping into someone's shoes entirely, not just standing nearby.

This is subtly different from simply saying "instead of you." Consider:

  • "She spoke instead of him" — simple substitution, she spoke, he didn't.
  • "She spoke in his stead" — she took on his role and spoke with the authority or responsibility that was his.

The second carries more weight and ceremony.

If you can remember that "instead" means "in (its) place," you've already understood the soul of this idiom.

"In someone's stead" = "instead of someone" — just more formal, and applied specifically to a person or thing being replaced.
"In someone's/something's stead" means doing what that person or thing was supposed to do — standing in their place, taking on their role, acting as their substitute.
8289:
"In spades" means in very large amounts, to a very great degree, or more than enough. It is used to intensify or emphasize whatever it is describing — almost like adding the words "a whole lot" or "big time" to a sentence.

Think of it as a powerful booster word. When you say someone has a quality "in spades," you are saying they have it abundantly — not just a little, not just enough, but far more than the average person.

Examples:

  • "She has patience in spades."
    She has a tremendous amount of patience.
  • "The new restaurant has atmosphere in spades."
    The restaurant has a wonderfully strong, rich atmosphere.
  • "He returned her generosity in spades."
    He gave back even more than she originally gave him.
  • "After the storm, we had problems in spades."
    We had a huge number of problems after the storm.

The idiom comes from card games — specifically from the suit of spades in a standard deck of playing cards.

In many popular card games, particularly Bridge (a very well-known card game), the four suits — hearts, diamonds, clubs, and spades — are not equal. They are ranked. Spades is the highest-ranking suit. It outranks all others. When a card from the spades suit appears, it beats cards from every other suit. Spades, in other words, represents the maximum, the most powerful, the highest value.

Over time, people began using "in spades" in everyday speech to mean "in the highest possible amount" or "with great strength" — just like how a spade card dominates all others in the game.

The phrase became common in American English in the early 20th century and has been widely used ever since.
The Grammar of This Idiom (How It Is Built)

This is important for a learner to know. "In spades" always comes after the thing it is describing. This is called a postpositive position. You cannot put it before.

Correct:

  • "She has talent in spades."
  • "They have problems in spades."

Incorrect:

  • ❌ "She has in spades talent."
  • ❌ "In spades they have problems."

The structure is always:

Subject + verb + noun/quality + "in spades"
The Tone — When and How People Use It

1. It is informal. This is a casual, everyday expression. You would use it in conversation, in casual writing, in journalism, or in storytelling — not in a formal essay or legal document.

2. It can be used positively or negatively. This is a key point many learners miss. The idiom itself is neutral — it simply means "a lot." The emotion (good or bad) comes from whatever word it is attached to.

  • Positive: "She has charisma in spades." (Great thing — lots of charisma!)
  • Negative: "The project had complications in spades." (Bad thing — lots of complications.)

3. It often carries a sense of admiration or surprise. When people say something exists "in spades," there is often a feeling of being impressed or slightly overwhelmed by the sheer quantity or intensity of it.

4. It is mainly used in American English, though speakers of British English and other varieties understand it well.
A Closely Related Meaning — "Repaid in Spades"

There is a slightly different but connected usage where "in spades" means returned or repaid with much more than was originally given. Like interest on a loan — you get back far more than you put in.

  • "I helped him once, and he repaid me in spades."
    He helped me back many more times than I helped him.
  • "Her hard work paid off in spades."
    Her hard work resulted in far more reward than expected.

This meaning is still rooted in the same idea of excess and abundance — you don't just get something back, you get it back multiplied.
How It Compares to Similar Expressions

Understanding related phrases will sharpen your grasp of this one:

  • "In abundance" — means having a lot of something, but is more formal and neutral in tone. "In spades" is more colorful and emphatic.
  • "Big time" — informal, similar energy. "He messed up big time" ≈ "He messed up in spades."
  • "In droves" — means in very large numbers, but is specifically used for people or things arriving/coming. "In spades" is more broadly used.
  • "To the hilt" — means to the maximum degree, but has a slightly different flavor. Both are emphatic intensifiers.

None of these are perfect substitutes — "in spades" has its own lively, punchy personality that is hard to fully replace.
One Thing to Be Aware Of

The word "spade" on its own has, at times in history, been used as an offensive racial slur. However, the idiom "in spades" is completely separate from this. It comes purely from card game terminology and predates the slur. Linguists and style guides widely consider "in spades" to be a normal, acceptable idiom with no offensive meaning. Most educated speakers use it freely and without concern. That said, it is good for you as a learner to simply be aware of this history, so you are never caught off guard if someone mentions it.

QuestionAnswer

In simple terms: "in spades" = a great deal of something, in very large or impressive amounts. It comes from card games where spades is the most powerful suit. It always follows the word or phrase it describes. It can describe good things or bad things. It is informal, vivid, and emphatic — a way of saying something doesn't just exist, it exists overwhelmingly.
8290:
"In spite of" means: something happened, even though there was an obstacle that could have prevented it.

The phrase points to a real difficulty, problem, or opposing fact — and then says: that thing was there, but it didn't stop the result.

Think of it this way: there's a wall (the obstacle), and there's a destination (the result). "In spite of" says the wall was real, you saw it, but you still reached the destination anyway.

"In spite of the heavy rain, they went for a walk."

The rain was the obstacle. Going for a walk was the result. The rain should have stopped them — but it didn't.

"She passed the exam in spite of not studying."

Not studying was the obstacle. Passing was the result. You'd normally expect not studying to cause failure — but she passed anyway.

"He smiled in spite of the pain."

The pain was real. The smile happened anyway.

In every case, the structure is the same:

In spite of [the obstacle] — [the result that happened anyway].
Where can it sit in a sentence?

"In spite of" can go at the beginning or in the middle of a sentence — both are correct, and both mean exactly the same thing.

  • "In spite of the noise, I slept well."
  • "I slept well in spite of the noise."

When it comes at the beginning, a comma usually follows the phrase before the main part of the sentence starts.
What must come after "in spite of"?

This is important grammar. "In spite of" must always be followed by:

  • A noun: in spite of the cold, in spite of the delay, in spite of his advice
  • A pronoun: in spite of it, in spite of everything, in spite of them
  • A verb+ing (called a gerund): in spite of being tired, in spite of knowing the truth, in spite of trying hard

It cannot be followed by a full clause (subject + verb). This is wrong:

✗ "In spite of he was tired, he kept going."

If you want to use a full sentence after it, you need a small fix — add "the fact that":

✓ "In spite of the fact that he was tired, he kept going."

Or switch to "although" or "even though," which are designed for full clauses:

✓ "Although he was tired, he kept going."
"In spite of" vs. "despite" — are they the same?

Yes, completely. They are interchangeable. "Despite" is simply one word that does the exact same job as "in spite of."

"In spite of the traffic, we arrived on time."
"Despite the traffic, we arrived on time."

Same meaning. Same grammar. You can use whichever you prefer. "Despite" is slightly more compact; "in spite of" can sometimes feel slightly more emphatic — but in everyday use, nobody will notice a difference.

These words express the same idea of contrast, but their grammar is different.

  • "In spite of" → followed by a noun or gerund (a thing, not a sentence)
  • "Although / Even though" → followed by a full clause (subject + verb)

Same meaning, different form:

"In spite of the cold weather, he wore a t-shirt."
"Although the weather was cold, he wore a t-shirt."

So if you find yourself writing "in spite of" and the next word is a subject (like "he," "she," "it," "the weather"), switch to "although" or "even though."

"In spite of" doesn't just show contrast — it acknowledges the obstacle. The speaker is not ignoring the difficulty. They are saying: "Yes, I see that thing. And still — it did not win."

This is why "in spite of" can make a result feel more impressive, more surprising, or more unfortunate, depending on context.

"She won the gold medal in spite of her injury."

→ The win feels more remarkable because the injury was real.

"He failed in spite of all his hard work."

→ The failure feels more painful because the effort was real.

Notice that "in spite of" can work in both directions — highlighting a positive result that defeated something bad, or a negative result that happened even when things seemed favorable.

"In spite of everything"
This means: even though many things stood in the way.

"In spite of everything, they remained close friends."

"In spite of yourself"
This is a well-known fixed expression. It means you did something even though you didn't intend to or didn't want to.

"She found herself laughing in spite of herself."

→ She didn't want to laugh (maybe the situation was serious), but she laughed anyway. She couldn't help it.

"He started to enjoy the movie in spite of himself."

→ He expected not to like it, maybe even resisted liking it — but he enjoyed it anyway.
